The trams of Lisbon

By Ana Ferreira

Lisbon's yellow trams have climbed the steep streets of the old town for more than a century. The famous line 28 winds from Martim Moniz through Graça and Alfama to Estrela, passing the cathedral and some of the narrowest curves of any city tram network in Europe.

The first electric trams ran in 1901, replacing horse-drawn cars that had served the city since 1873. Today the remodelled cars from the 1930s still run on the hilly lines, because modern vehicles are too long for the tight bends. Read more in our history of the network.

Riding line 28

Visitors are advised to board early in the morning, when the cars are less crowded. A single ticket bought on board costs more than a day pass, which is also valid on buses, the funiculars and the Santa Justa lift. Pickpockets are common on the busiest stretches, so keep your belongings close.

The city plans to renew part of the fleet in the coming years while keeping the historic cars on the steepest lines, a balance between the needs of residents and the visitors who come for the ride itself.
